myth: Myth: an AI chatbot looks the answer up on the internet.
reality: Reality: a language model writes likely text from patterns it learned in training. Some products add search or document lookup on top.
so_what: So when a tool does not show sources, treat the answer as a draft to check.
do: Ask: 'Did you search for this, or are you answering from training?'

myth: Myth: if an AI sounds confident, it is probably right.
reality: Reality: models can produce confident-sounding statements that are false or unsupported. This is called a hallucination.
so_what: Confidence of tone tells you nothing about accuracy.
do: Check names, numbers and quotes against a source before you use them.

myth: Myth: an AI that only reads a web page cannot be tricked by it.
reality: Reality: text on a page can contain instructions aimed at the model. This is called prompt injection, and it is listed among the main security risks for AI applications.
so_what: Anything an AI reads from outside is untrusted input.
do: Be careful when an AI tool can browse, read email or open files and then take actions.

myth: Myth: you have to retrain an AI to make it use your documents.
reality: Reality: retrieval-augmented generation lets a model look up relevant documents at answer time, without retraining it.
so_what: Retrieval is often the first thing to try for company documents.
do: Ask what a product retrieves, and whether it shows you the passages it used.

myth: Myth: a smaller AI model is always much worse than a bigger one.
reality: Reality: in knowledge distillation a smaller model is trained to imitate a larger one, aiming to keep much of its ability at lower cost.
so_what: Size is one factor, not the whole story.
do: Test a smaller model on your own task before you pay for a bigger one.
